title: ManifoldCache: Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration via Constraint Manifold Caching

paper.title: ManifoldCache: Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration via Constraint Manifold Caching
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion models for structured scientific generation must produce
samples satisfying hard geometric constraints imposed by physics,
chemistry, or biology, yet inference in these settings is
prohibitively slow, demanding hundreds to thousands of neural-function
evaluations per sample.
We unify eight state-of-the-art models spanning medical volumetrics,
molecular conformations, protein backbone design, crystal structure
prediction, and multi-view 3D scenes under a single abstraction, Constraint-Manifold Diffusion Models (CMDMs), in
which the target distribution is supported on a manifold defined by
an externally specified constraint map.
Existing acceleration families transfer poorly to this class: quantization
exhausts memory on high-dimensional volumetric operators; pruning
breaks constraint fidelity; fast ODE solvers allow trajectories to
drift off the constraint manifold; and feature-caching heuristics are
blind to constraint geometry and can cause mode confusion in the
high-noise regime.
We introduce ManifoldCache , the first training-free,
data-free accelerator designed from first principles for CMDMs.
The key insight is that the conditional score decomposes orthogonally
into a normal component, which enforces constraint satisfaction, and a
tangential component, which navigates within the manifold.
Building on this structure, we show for a two-mode Gaussian model
that the noise-schedule midpoint, where signal and noise have equal
energy, separates two regimes: once signal dominates, the error of a
cached estimate is provably bounded, while before that point a
strictly positive fraction of cached estimates land in the wrong mode,
and this fraction does not vanish as the midpoint is approached.
We further prove that, under an explicit condition on the balance
between the two score components, deeper network blocks admit larger
certified cache strides, as a consequence of the score decomposition
propagating through block Jacobians.
The resulting schedule requires one integer comparison per block per
step, zero calibration data, and zero training overhead.
Across all eight CMDMs, ManifoldCache delivers wall-clock
speedups of 1.2 1.2 – 1.9 × 1.9\times and stays closest to full-inference
quality on each model’s primary metric among the feature-caching
methods we compare; on Med-DDPM it also offers a better
quality–speed trade-off than quantization, pruning, and fast-solver
baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/prinshul/Manifoldcache.git .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models have transformed generative modelling across images ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ) , audio ( Kong et al., 2020 ) , and video ( Ho et al., 2022 ) . Their most consequential frontier lies in the structured spaces of science and engineering: volumetric anatomical atlases ( Dorjsembe et al., 2024 ) , molecular conformations and graphs ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Frank et al., 2026 ; Kong et al., 2025 ) , protein backbones ( Geffner et al., 2025 ) , periodic crystal lattices ( Jiao et al., 2024 ) , and multi-view 3D scenes ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Bahmani et al., 2026 ) . What unites these applications is the fact that their target distributions are supported not on the full ambient space 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , but on a constraint manifold ℳ c = { x ∈ 𝒳 : g ⁡ ( x , c ) = 0 } \mathcal{M}_{c}=\{x\in\mathcal{X}:g(x;c)=0\} , where the constraint map g g encodes physics, chemistry, geometry, or biology. We call this class Constraint-Manifold Diffusion Models ( CMDMs ). CMDMs are central to drug discovery ( Kong et al., 2025 ) , de novo protein design ( Geffner et al., 2025 ) , and crystal structure prediction ( Jiao et al., 2024 ) , yet inference is prohibitively slow: Med-DDPM ( Dorjsembe et al., 2024 ) requires 2 min 45 sec per sample on a single A100 GPU, demanding hundreds to thousands of neural-function evaluations (NFEs). Figure 1: Quality–speed trade-off on Med-DDPM ( Dorjsembe et al., 2024 ) across quantization, pruning, solver, and caching baselines. ManifoldCache achieves 1 min 31 sec per sample (full inference: 2 min 45 sec); all baselines either degrade quality, slow down, or incur OOM. Why existing methods fall short on CMDMs. CMDMs employ fundamentally different backbone architectures (volumetric convolutions, SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) -equivariant networks, graph transformers), whose feature dynamics are poorly matched by heuristics designed for pixel-space UNets and vision transformers. Post-training quantization ( Shang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2023 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) requires a calibration pass that exhausts GPU memory on volumetric operators such as the Conv3D layers in Med-DDPM. Pruning ( Han et al., 2015 ; Fang et al., 2023 ) removes weights that collectively enforce g g ; even 30% sparsity produces samples violating hard geometric constraints. Faster ODE solvers ( Song et al., 2020 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) exploit trajectory smoothness that holds only in the clean limit; large steps allow drift off ℳ c \mathcal{M}_{c} , and for discrete-diffusion variants ( Liu et al., 2026 ) they are categorically inapplicable. Feature-caching methods (DeepCache ( Ma et al., 2024 ) , SmoothCache ( Liu et al., 2025c ) , TeaCache ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , FORA ( Selvaraju et al., 2024 ) , and others) exploit near-stationarity of activations but apply cache-trigger rules blind to constraint geometry, causing over-caching (collapsing constraint fidelity) or under-caching (negligible speedup). Crucially, none identifies the schedule midpoint α ¯ t = 1 2 \bar{\alpha}_{t}=\tfrac{1}{2} as a safe-caching boundary, and none assigns block-level strides from depth-dependent score structure. We propose ManifoldCache , the first inference-acceleration framework for CMDMs, derived from the orthogonal decomposition of the conditional score into a normal component s t ⟂ s_{t}^{\perp} (enforcing constraint satisfaction) and a tangential component s t ∥ s_{t}^{\parallel} (navigating along ℳ c \mathcal{M}_{c} ). Theorem 1 shows, for a two-mode Gaussian model, that T ∗ = max ⁡ { t : α ¯ t ≥ 1 2 } T^{*}=\max\{t:\bar{\alpha}_{t}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\} , which depends only on the noise schedule, separates two regimes: for τ ≤ T ∗ \tau\leq T^{*} the expected squared error of the frozen Tweedie estimate is at most 1 2 ​ tr ⁡ Σ c \tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{c} and the probability of landing in the wrong mode is small for well-separated modes, while for τ > T ∗ \tau>T^{*} a strictly positive fraction of frozen estimates lands in the wrong manifold mode for every within-mode spread. Theorem 2 establishes that within the safe phase, deeper network blocks admit provably larger certified cache strides, as a formal consequence of the score decomposition propagating through block Jacobians when the normal-to-tangential power ratio κ t \kappa_{t} falls below an explicit threshold κ ∗ \kappa^{*} . ManifoldCache instantiates both results as a lightweight, training-free schedule: one integer comparison per block per step, zero calibration, zero training overhead. On Med-DDPM this yields ≈ 1.8 × {\approx}1.8\times wall-clock speedup with the lowest FID among the caching methods we compare (Figure 1 , Table 5 ). Contributions. (1) A unified framework (§ 3.1 ) showing that eight state-of-the-art models (Med-DDPM ( Dorjsembe et al., 2024 ) , SV4D 2.0 ( Yao et al., 2025 ) , DemoDiff ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , Proteina ( Geffner et al., 2025 ) , DiT-MC ( Frank et al., 2026 ) , UniMoMo ( Kong et al., 2025 ) , DiffCSP++ ( Jiao et al., 2024 ) , Lyra ( Bahmani et al., 2026 ) ) are all special cases of the CMDM construction. (2) A schedule-derived safe-caching threshold T ∗ T^{*} (Theorem 1 , § 3.3 ) that separates a regime of provably bounded caching error from one with a provably non-vanishing mode-flip probability, depending only on the noise schedule. (3) Depth-monotone cacheability via Jacobian decomposition (Theorem 2 , § 3.4 ), providing the first theoretical justification for depth-adaptive caching with an explicit regime condition. (4) ManifoldCache (§ 3.4 , Figure 1 ), which on seven of the eight CMDMs is faster than every baseline while scoring best among the accelerators on the primary quality metric.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Constraint-manifold diffusion models. A growing class of diffusion models generates samples satisfying hard geometric, physical, or biological constraints ( Dorjsembe et al., 2024 ; Jiao et al., 2024 ; Yao et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Geffner et al., 2025 ; Frank et al., 2026 ; Kong et al., 2025 ) . Their backbones (volumetric 3D ConvNets, SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) -equivariant networks, graph transformers, and multi-view ViTs) are heavier than standard 2D UNets; constraint fidelity degrades sharply under step reduction since the probability flow is only tangent to ℳ c \mathcal{M}_{c} in the clean limit; and guidance strategies multiply NFEs by 2–4 × \times . Together, these factors significantly increase the inference and generation times for CMDMs. Acceleration methods. Post-training quantization ( Shang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2023 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) reduces per-step compute via INT8/FP8/INT4 weight and activation compression. On volumetric CMDMs, calibration passes exhaust GPU memory, resulting in Out of Memory (OOM) (mainly block reconstruction approaches), and quantization noise accumulates along directions normal to ℳ c \mathcal{M}_{c} , where any error directly manifests as constraint violation. Pruning. Magnitude ( Han et al., 2015 ) and structural ( Fang et al., 2023 ) pruning remove low-saliency weights to reduce per-step cost. On CMDMs every weight participates in satisfying the constraint map g g ; 30% sparsity already drives generation quality below an acceptable level, and neither variant reduces the NFE count. Fast solvers. DDIM ( Song et al., 2020 ) and DPM-Solver++ ( Lu et al., 2025 ) reduce NFEs by taking larger probability-flow ODE integration steps, exploiting trajectory smoothness in unconstrained image models. On CMDMs, large steps allow trajectories to drift off ℳ c \mathcal{M}_{c} before any corrective force restores them, producing constraint-violating samples. For discrete-diffusion variants such as DemoDiff ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , which operate on token simplices, high-order ODE solvers are categorically inapplicable. Feature caching. DeepCache ( Ma et al., 2024 ) , FasterDiffusion ( Li et al., 2024 ) , FORA ( Selvaraju et al., 2024 ) , SmoothCache ( Liu et al., 2025c ) , TeaCache ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , AB-Cache ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , PFC ( Sommer et al., 2025 ) , ToCa ( Zou et al., 2024 ) , dKV-Cache ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , TaylorSeer ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , PAB ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) , AdaCache ( Kahatapitiya et al., 2025 ) , and FrDiff ( So et al., 2024 ) exploit the near-stationarity of hidden activations between adjacent denoising steps via fixed intervals, calibration thresholds, input-difference proxies, or numerical extrapolation. These methods share a common limitation: none uses the geometric structure of ℳ c \mathcal{M}_{c} as a caching criterion, and none identifies α ¯ t = 1 2 \bar{\alpha}_{t}=\tfrac{1}{2} as a safe-caching boundary, so they may reuse features in the high-noise phase where, as Theorem 1 shows for a two-mode model, the modes are not yet resolved and reuse leads to mode confusion with non-vanishing probability. ManifoldCache is the first framework to derive a depth-adaptive caching schedule with provable error bounds from constraint geometry, requiring no training, no calibration data, and no per-step runtime measurement. Speculative sampling. Speculative methods for diffusion models ( De Bortoli et al., 2025 ) and diffusion language models ( Agrawal et al., 2025 ) draft future denoising states with a cheaper proposal and then accept or reject them in a verification step, which reduces the number of expensive model calls while preserving the output distribution. ManifoldCache works on a different axis: it keeps every denoising step and lowers the cost of each step by reusing block outputs according to a fixed schedule, with no draft model or verifier. The two approaches are therefore complementary; Appendix E discusses the differences in more detail and compares them on Proteina.

sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.text: ManifoldCache rests on a single observation: the physics or biology that defines a constraint manifold also determines when and where a denoiser’s computation can be safely skipped. We formalise this in four steps: (i) defining the CMDM class, (ii) decomposing the score geometrically, (iii) deriving a universal safe-caching threshold, and (iv) assembling a closed-form depth-adaptive schedule. Figure 2 illustrates the main ideas. Figure 2: Geometric picture behind ManifoldCache . (a) Near ℳ c \mathcal{M}_{c} , the score splits into a normal part s t ⟂ s_{t}^{\perp} , which pulls the sample toward ℳ c \mathcal{M}_{c} , and a tangential part s t ∥ s_{t}^{\parallel} , which moves it within ℳ c \mathcal{M}_{c} toward one of the valid modes (here μ 1 \mu_{1} and μ 2 \mu_{2} , separated by δ c \delta_{c} ; § 3.2 ). (b) The threshold T ∗ = max ⁡ { t : α ¯ t ≥ 1 2 } T^{*}=\max\{t:\bar{\alpha}_{t}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\} splits the schedule: for t > T ∗ t>T^{*} every block is recomputed, and caching is enabled only for t ≤ T ∗ t\leq T^{*} (Theorem 1 ); the κ t \kappa_{t} curve is schematic. (c) For t ≤ T ∗ t\leq T^{*} , the cache stride grows with block depth (Eq. ( 6 )): shallow blocks are recomputed often, and deep blocks are reused for longer.

sections.heading: 3.1 Constraint-Manifold Diffusion Models
sections.text: Let 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ D \mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{D} be the ambient space , a voxel grid, sequence of residue coordinates, periodic unit cell, or latent video tensor depending on the application. Structured generative models do not place mass freely across 𝒳 \mathcal{X} ; they confine samples to a surface carved out by domain knowledge. Definition 1 (CMDM) . A Constraint-Manifold Diffusion Model is specified by a C 2 C^{2} constraint map g : 𝒳 × 𝒞 → ℝ k g:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathbb{R}^{k} and a conditioning signal c ∈ 𝒞 c\in\mathcal{C} . The target distribution p ( ⋅ ∣ c ) p(\cdot\mid c) is supported on the constraint manifold ℳ c := { x ∈ 𝒳 : g ⁡ ( x , c ) = 0 } \mathcal{M}_{c}:=\{x\in\mathcal{X}:g(x;c)=0\} . We assume ∇ x g ​ ( x , c ) \nabla_{x}g(x;c) has full rank k k at every x ∈ ℳ c x\in\mathcal{M}_{c} (submersion condition), so by the Implicit Function Theorem ℳ c \mathcal{M}_{c} is a closed C 2 C^{2} submanifold of 𝒳 \mathcal{X} of dimension d c := D − k d_{c}:=D-k . State-of-the-art CMDM models across various domains are special cases: Med-DDPM ( Dorjsembe et al., 2024 ) ( 𝒳 = ℝ 192 3 \mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^{192^{3}} , g g enforces anatomical intensity and continuity), DiffCSP++ ( Jiao et al., 2024 ) ( g g encodes crystallographic space-group symmetry), Proteina ( Geffner et al., 2025 ) ( 𝒳 = ℝ 3 ​ N \mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^{3N} , the C α C_{\alpha} coordinates of N N residues; g g encodes Ramachandran validity and steric clash avoidance), SV4D 2.0 ( Yao et al., 2025 ) and Lyra ( Bahmani et al., 2026 ) ( g g imposes multi-view photometric consistency). Despite radically different ambient spaces, all share three properties our theory exploits: g g is externally specified, not learned (P1) ; codimension k ≫ 1 k\gg 1 so a random point in 𝒳 \mathcal{X} violates the constraints with probability approaching one (P2) ; and c c is exact at every diffusion step (P3) . The constraint map g g describes where the data lie: it is a modelling assumption about the support of p ( ⋅ ∣ c ) p(\cdot\mid c) , not an operation performed at inference. ManifoldCache never evaluates g g , projects onto ℳ c \mathcal{M}_{c} , or checks constraint satisfaction; it reads only the timestep and the block index. How a model keeps its samples on ℳ c \mathcal{M}_{c} (through training data, conditioning, or an architecture that builds the constraint in) therefore does not affect how the schedule is applied. Table 9 in Appendix B lists the constraint and this mechanism for each of the eight models.

sections.heading: 4.1 Models, Datasets, and Metrics
sections.text: We evaluate ManifoldCache on eight CMDMs (§ 3.1 ) across five scientific domains using official open-source checkpoints. Med-DDPM ( Dorjsembe et al., 2024 ) is a Conv3D U-Net DDPM for segmentation-conditioned semantic 3D brain MRI synthesis on 192 × 192 × 192 192{\times}192{\times}192 BraTS 2021 volumes, evaluated with volumetric 3D FID . SV4D 2.0 ( Yao et al., 2025 ) is a multi-view video diffusion transformer with joint 3D/frame attention for monocular-video-to-4D asset generation, evaluated on Objaverse ( Yao et al., 2025 ) over 8 8 view pairs using PSNR , SSIM , and LPIPS , computed against full inference (§ 5 ). Lyra ( Bahmani et al., 2026 ) is an NVIDIA self-distilled video diffusion model featuring a camera-controlled GEN3C-based video DiT for single-image-to-3D Gaussian Splatting scene generation, evaluated using rendered novel views with PSNR , SSIM , and LPIPS , computed against full inference (§ 5 ). Proteina ( Geffner et al., 2025 ) is a 200M-parameter non-equivariant flow-matching transformer for hierarchical-CATH-conditioned C α C_{\alpha} protein backbone generation trained on AFDB+PDB, evaluated by the ProteinMPNN → \rightarrow ESMFold self-consistency pipeline using mean scRMSD , where scRMSD < 2 {<}2 Å denotes designable samples. DiT-MC ( Frank et al., 2026 ) adapts diffusion transformers to graph-conditioned 3D molecular conformer generation and is evaluated on GEOM-QM9 using mean COV-R and COV-P at 0.75 0.75 Å RMSD. UniMoMo ( Kong et al., 2025 ) is an E(3)-equivariant geometric latent diffusion model for unified peptide, antibody, and small-molecule binder generation from block-graph representations, evaluated on PepBench using mean AAR , median C-RMSD , and median L-RMSD . DiffCSP++ ( Jiao et al., 2024 ) is a periodic equivariant diffusion model jointly denoising lattices, fractional coordinates, and atom types under explicit space-group/Wyckoff constraints for crystal structure prediction, evaluated on MP-20 with Match Rate and RMSD . DemoDiff ( Liu et al., 2026 ) is a 0.7 0.7 B-parameter discrete graph diffusion transformer for in-context molecular design on Node-Pair-Encoding motif-tokenised graphs, pretrained on 1.6 1.6 M ChEMBL+polymer tasks and evaluated on its 33-task benchmark using task-averaged Score and ICL Consistency Score ( Liu et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced ManifoldCache , the first training-free acceleration framework designed specifically for Constraint-Manifold Diffusion Models (CMDMs). By exploiting the orthogonal decomposition of the diffusion score into manifold-normal and manifold-tangential components, ManifoldCache derives a principled safe-caching threshold directly from the noise schedule together with a depth-adaptive caching policy grounded in score geometry. The resulting method requires no retraining, no calibration data, and negligible runtime overhead. Across eight diverse CMDMs spanning medical imaging, molecular generation, protein design, crystal prediction, and multi-view 4D synthesis, ManifoldCache consistently achieves superior quality–speed trade-offs and often simultaneously improves both inference time and generation fidelity over strong existing accelerators. Our results suggest that constraint geometry is not only central to generation quality, but also a fundamental signal for determining when and where diffusion computation can be safely reused.

sections.heading: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.text: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: This can be verified by the abstract and introduction. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: In the Appendix Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes] Justification: In the appendix Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Implementation details added Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Datasets are public, settings and splits are provided, code will be released upon acceptance Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. • Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark). • The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. • The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. • At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). • Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Details provided in the main paper Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. • The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [N/A] Justification: All existing methods in this category report numbers without error bars, so we followed them. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). • If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Provided in main paper Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. • The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. • The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines ? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper conforms to the Code of Ethics. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. • If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics. • The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [N/A] Justification: There is no societal impact of the work performed. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. • If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. • Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. • The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. • The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. • If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper poses no such risks. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. • Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. • Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. • We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We have referenced the required papers. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. • The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. • The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL. • The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. • For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. • If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset. • For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. • If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [N/A] Justification: There are no new assets. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. • Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. • The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. • At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. • Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper. • According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector. 15. Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. • Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper. • We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution. • For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review. 16. Declaration of LLM usage Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required. Answer: [Yes] Justification: Used for writing and editing etc. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components. • Please refer to our LLM policy in the NeurIPS handbook for what should or should not be described.

sections.heading: Appendix E Comparison with Speculative Sampling
sections.text: Speculative methods and ManifoldCache reduce cost in different ways. Speculative methods reduce the number of expensive model calls: a cheap proposal drafts future states, and the target model then accepts or rejects them, which keeps the samples exactly distributed as those of the target model [ De Bortoli et al., 2025 , Agrawal et al., 2025 ] . ManifoldCache has no draft model, verifier, or rejection step. It keeps every denoising step and lowers the cost of each one by reusing block outputs according to a fixed schedule that depends only on the noise level and the block depth. This leads to three practical differences. First, speculative methods need either a separate draft model, which is costly to obtain for 3D MRI or protein generation, or additional machinery. The training-free drafts of De Bortoli et al. [2025] require a stochastic sampler (the authors note that their method does not apply directly to deterministic samplers), and Spiffy [ Agrawal et al., 2025 ] calibrates its draft graphs offline for discrete diffusion language models. De Bortoli et al. [2025] also note that, unlike large language models, diffusion models are not necessarily memory-bound, so parallel verification may bring smaller wall-clock gains. ManifoldCache needs no calibration and runs on all eight backbones. Second, the guarantees differ: speculative sampling preserves the output distribution of the target model, whereas ManifoldCache bounds the error of reuse and the probability of landing in the wrong mode (Theorem 1 ). Third, the two act on different parts of the trajectory: the analysis of De Bortoli et al. [2025] indicates that the acceptance rate is high at the beginning of denoising, which is the high-noise phase in which Theorem 1 advises against caching. In principle the two could therefore be combined, with speculation reducing the number of steps and caching reducing the cost of each remaining step; we leave this to future work. Table 12 compares both speculative methods with ManifoldCache on Proteina. Neither method was designed for continuous protein backbone generation, so both had to be adapted. In our adaptations, drafts are verified token by token, which captures the continuous dynamics poorly; drafts were therefore often rejected and rolled back, both runs were slower than full inference, and the resulting scRMSD was much higher. sections.heading: Appendix G Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: Despite strong empirical and theoretical performance, ManifoldCache has several important limitations that motivate future work. First, our theory relies on smooth closed manifold assumptions with well-defined tangent and normal decompositions. While these assumptions cover a broad range of scientific diffusion models, some structured generation problems involve non-smooth, discrete, combinatorial, or dynamically changing constraint sets where the local geometric decomposition may not exist or may vary discontinuously across the trajectory. Extending manifold-aware caching to hybrid discrete–continuous diffusion processes, topology-changing manifolds, or non-Euclidean latent spaces remains an open direction . Second, the theoretical guarantees are derived under simplified regularity and mixture assumptions designed to make the analysis tractable. Real CMDMs exhibit highly multimodal, non-Gaussian, and hierarchical distributions whose geometry may evolve across denoising stages. Although the ablations support the choice of T ∗ T^{*} , deriving sharper guarantees under more realistic score models, heavy-tailed distributions, or learned manifold geometries would strengthen the theoretical foundations of geometry-aware acceleration . In addition, the depth ordering of Theorem 2 relies on the regime condition κ t < κ ∗ \kappa_{t}<\kappa^{*} , which we assume rather than derive. Third, the current schedule is analytically fixed from the noise schedule and block depth and does not adapt online to individual samples, prompts, or trajectory difficulty. Certain trajectories may approach the manifold substantially earlier or later than predicted by the global schedule, especially in highly multimodal settings. Future work could investigate sample-adaptive or uncertainty-aware caching policies that dynamically estimate manifold proximity, score curvature, or feature drift during inference while retaining the low-overhead nature of the current framework . Fourth, although ManifoldCache is backbone-agnostic, the present implementation focuses on inference-time feature reuse and does not jointly optimize with other acceleration mechanisms such as learned schedulers, consistency distillation, speculative denoising, low-rank adaptation, or mixed-precision execution. Combining geometry-aware caching with solver acceleration, quantization, or token sparsification could potentially yield multiplicative speedups beyond those observed here . Fifth, our experiments focus on single-device inference on existing pretrained checkpoints. Large-scale distributed generation systems introduce additional communication and synchronization bottlenecks that may alter the trade-off between recomputation and cache reuse. Investigating geometry-aware caching under tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, or streaming generation settings is an important systems-level extension . Finally, our work studies geometry primarily as a mechanism for safe acceleration. A broader future direction is to treat manifold structure as a unifying principle connecting controllability, robustness, interpretability, and efficiency in scientific generative models . We believe CMDMs provide a promising foundation for studying these properties jointly, particularly in emerging multimodal settings combining physical simulation, language conditioning, molecular reasoning, and embodied 3D generation.

We unify eight state-of-the-art models spanning medical volumetrics, molecular conformations, protein backbone design, crystal structure prediction, and multi-view 3D scenes under a single abstraction, Constraint-Manifold Diffusion Models (CMDMs), in which the target distribution is supported on a manifold defined by an externally specified constraint map. Existing acceleration families transfer poorly to this class: quantization exhausts memory on high-dimensional volumetric operators; pruning breaks constraint fidelity; fast ODE solvers allow trajectories to drift off the constraint manifold; and feature-caching heuristics are blind to constraint geometry and can cause mode confusion in the high-noise regime. We introduce ManifoldCache , the first training-free, data-free accelerator designed from first principles for CMDMs. The key insight is that the conditional score decomposes orthogonally into a normal component, which enforces constraint satisfaction, and a tangential component, which navigates within the manifold. Building on this structure, we show for a two-mode Gaussian model that the noise-schedule midpoint, where signal and noise have equal energy, separates two regimes: once signal dominates, the error of a cached estimate is provably bounded, while before that point a strictly positive fraction of cached estimates land in the wrong mode, and this fraction does not vanish as the midpoint is approached. We further prove that, under an explicit condition on the balance between the two score components, deeper network blocks admit larger certified cache strides, as a consequence of the score decomposition propagating through block Jacobians. The resulting schedule requires one integer comparison per block per step, zero calibration data, and zero training overhead. Across all eight CMDMs, ManifoldCache delivers wall-clock speedups of 1.2 1.2 – 1.9 × 1.9	imes and stays closest to full-inference quality on each model’s primary metric among the feature-caching methods we compare; on Med-DDPM it also offers a better quality–speed trade-off than quantization, pruning, and fast-solver baselines. Their most consequential frontier lies in the structured spaces of science and engineering: volumetric anatomical atlases ( Dorjsembe et al., 2024 ) , molecular conformations and graphs ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Frank et al., 2026 ; Kong et al., 2025 ) , protein backbones ( Geffner et al., 2025 ) , periodic crystal lattices ( Jiao et al., 2024 ) , and multi-view 3D scenes ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Bahmani et al., 2026 ) . We call this class Constraint-Manifold Diffusion Models ( CMDMs ). CMDMs are central to drug discovery ( Kong et al., 2025 ) , de novo protein design ( Geffner et al., 2025 ) , and crystal structure prediction ( Jiao et al., 2024 ) , yet inference is prohibitively slow: Med-DDPM ( Dorjsembe et al., 2024 ) requires 2 min 45 sec per sample on a single A100 GPU, demanding hundreds to thousands of neural-function evaluations (NFEs). A growing class of diffusion models generates samples satisfying hard geometric, physical, or biological constraints ( Dorjsembe et al., 2024 ; Jiao et al., 2024 ; Yao et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Geffner et al., 2025 ; Frank et al., 2026 ; Kong et al., 2025 ) . Their backbones (volumetric 3D ConvNets, SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) -equivariant networks, graph transformers, and multi-view ViTs) are heavier than standard 2D UNets; constraint fidelity degrades sharply under step reduction since the probability flow is only tangent to ℳ c \mathcal{M}_{c} in the clean limit; and guidance strategies multiply NFEs by 2–4 × 	imes . Together, these factors significantly increase the inference and generation times for CMDMs. Acceleration methods. Post-training quantization ( Shang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2023 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) reduces per-step compute via INT8/FP8/INT4 weight and activation compression. On volumetric CMDMs, calibration passes exhaust GPU memory, resulting in Out of Memory (OOM) (mainly block reconstruction approaches), and quantization noise accumulates along directions normal to ℳ c \mathcal{M}_{c} , where any error directly manifests as constraint violation. Pruning. Magnitude ( Han et al., 2015 ) and structural ( Fang et al., 2023 ) pruning remove low-saliency weights to reduce per-step cost. On CMDMs every weight participates in satisfying the constraint map g g ; 30% sparsity already drives generation quality below an acceptable level, and neither variant reduces the NFE count. Fast solvers. DDIM ( Song et al., 2020 ) and DPM-Solver++ ( Lu et al., 2025 ) reduce NFEs by taking larger probability-flow ODE integration steps, exploiting trajectory smoothness in unconstrained image models. On CMDMs, large steps allow trajectories to drift off ℳ c \mathcal{M}_{c} before any corrective force restores them, producing constraint-violating samples. For discrete-diffusion variants such as DemoDiff ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , which operate on token simplices, high-order ODE solvers are categorically inapplicable. Feature caching. DeepCache ( Ma et al., 2024 ) , FasterDiffusion ( Li et al., 2024 ) , FORA ( Selvaraju et al., 2024 ) , SmoothCache ( Liu et al., 2025c ) , TeaCache ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , AB-Cache ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , PFC ( Sommer et al., 2025 ) , ToCa ( Zou et al., 2024 ) , dKV-Cache ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , TaylorSeer ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , PAB ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) , AdaCache ( Kahatapitiya et al., 2025 ) , and FrDiff ( So et al., 2024 ) exploit the near-stationarity of hidden activations between adjacent denoising steps via fixed intervals, calibration thresholds, input-difference proxies, or numerical extrapolation. These methods share a common limitation: none uses the geometric structure of ℳ c \mathcal{M}_{c} as a caching criterion, and none identifies α ¯ t = 1 2  ar{\alpha}_{t}=	frac{1}{2} as a safe-caching boundary, so they may reuse features in the high-noise phase where, as Theorem 1 shows for a two-mode model, the modes are not yet resolved and reuse leads to mode confusion with non-vanishing probability. ManifoldCache is the first framework to derive a depth-adaptive caching schedule with provable error bounds from constraint geometry, requiring no training, no calibration data, and no per-step runtime measurement. Speculative sampling. Speculative methods for diffusion models ( De Bortoli et al., 2025 ) and diffusion language models ( Agrawal et al., 2025 ) draft future denoising states with a cheaper proposal and then accept or reject them in a verification step, which reduces the number of expensive model calls while preserving the output distribution. ManifoldCache works on a different axis: it keeps every denoising step and lowers the cost of each step by reusing block outputs according to a fixed schedule, with no draft model or verifier.
